## Introduction

Here is an example of a conditional sentence in English:

(@ex001153) [If you come to me, then I will honor you.]{.trans}

@fig-cst_eng_ex1 shows its parts.

::: {#fig-cst_eng_ex1 .test-class}

The parts of a conditional sentence.
:::

As you can see,
a conditional sentence is a special sentence, which consists of two parts:

1. A _condition_ ([If you come to me]{.trans})
   The condition itself consists of two parts:

    i. The *conditional-device*: ([if]{.trans})
   ii. The *condition-core*: ([you come to me]{.trans})

2. A _condition-response_. ([then I will come to you]{.trans})
   The condition-response can also consist of two parts:

    i. The *condition-response-link*: ([then]{.trans}). This may be null for some conditional sentences.
   ii. The *condition-response-core*: ([I will honor you]{.trans})

There are many
_conditional-devices_
in Arabic.
Some common
ones
are:

* [إِنْ]{.ar} [if]{.trans}
* [إِذَا]{.ar} [when]{.trans}
* [لَوْ]{.ar} [if]{.trans}
* [مَنْ]{.ar} [who(ever)]{.trans}
* [مَا]{.ar} [what(ever)]{.trans}

We will study them in the following sections.

## The [إِنْ]{.ar} conditional sentence

[إِنْ]{.ar} is considered the most basic of all the conditional-devices.^[[[كتاب سيبويه]{.ar} 3/63](https://shamela.ws/book/23018/916); [[شرح ابن يعيش على المفصل]{.ar} 5/106](https://shamela.ws/book/13301/2044)]
<!--
It forms the basic conditional sentence.
Conditional sentences that employ other conditional-devices are based on
the conditional sentence with [إِنْ]{.ar}.
-->

There are a few different types of conditional sentence that can be formed with [إِنْ]{.ar}.
We will discuss them below:

<!--
is used to form the _archetypal_ conditional sentence.
Other types of conditional sentence are formed based on the
model of
archetypal conditional sentence with [إِنْ]{.ar}.
-->

### The archetypal [إِنْ]{.ar} conditional sentence {#sec-jsh_arch_in}

Here is an example of an archetypal,
or most basic, 
conditional sentence:

(@ex001154) [إِنْ يَأْتِ زَيْدٌ يُكْرِمْهُ عَمْرٌو]{.ar}  
    [If Zayd will come, [#eamr]{.trn2} will honor him.]{.trans}  

The archetypal, 
[إِنْ]{.ar} conditional sentence
uses
ø-case [muDArie]{.trn2} verbs in both the condition and the condition-response.
This conditional sentence consists of two parts:

1. a condition, ([إِنْ يَأْتِ زَيْدٌ]{.ar})  
   consisting of:
    i. the conditional-device ([إِنْ]{.ar}), and 
   ii. the condition-core
       ([يَأْتِ زَيْدٌ]{.ar}),
       which is a verbal sentence containing:
       * a ø-case [muDArie]{.trn2} verb known as the *condition-verb*
         ([يَأْتِ]{.ar})
       * its doer
         ([زَيْدٌ]{.ar})
2. a condition-response,
   ([يُكْرِمْهُ عَمْرٌو]{.ar})
   consisting of:
   i. the condition-response-core
      ([يُكْرِمْهُ عَمْرٌو]{.ar}),
      which is a verbal sentence containing:
      * a ø-case [muDArie]{.trn2} verb known as the *condition-response-verb*
        ([يُكْرِمْ]{.ar})
      * its doer
        ([عَمْرٌو]{.ar})

   There is no condition-response-link in the archetypal [إِنْ]{.ar} conditional sentence.

The conditional particle [إِنْ]{.ar} directly
governs the condition-verb and the condition-response-verb in the ø-case.^[Peled, _Conditional structures in Classical Arabic_ 3--4 citing [كتاب سيبويه]{.ar}]

Here are some more examples of the archetypal conditional sentence:

(@ex001156) [إِنْ تَأْتِنِي آتِكَ]{.ar}
    [[[كتاب سيبويه]{.ar} 3/63](https://shamela.ws/book/23018/916)]{.citex}  
    [If you will come to me, I will come to you.]{.trans}

(@ex001157) [إن تضرب أضرب]{.ar}
    [[[كتاب سيبويه]{.ar} 3/63](https://shamela.ws/book/23018/916)]{.citex}  
    [If you will beat, I will beat.]{.trans}

### The [mADI]{.trn2} verb with [إِنْ]{.ar} {#sec-jsh_qatala}

A [mADI]{.trn2} verb can be used instead of one or both of the ø-case verbs in a conditional sentence.
So, for example, instead of saying:

(@ex001158) [إِنْ تَأْتِنِي أُكْرِمْكَ]{.ar}

we can say, any one of:

(@ex001159) [إِنْ أَتَيْتَنِي أَكْرَمْتُكَ]{.ar}

(@ex001160) [إِنْ أَتَيْتَنِي أُكْرِمْكَ]{.ar}

(@ex001161) [إِنْ تَأْتِنِي أَكْرَمْتُكَ]{.ar}

As a matter of fact,
in terms of frequency of usage,
the [mADI]{.trn2} verb
is more common than the archetypal ø-case [muDArie]{.trn2} verb
in conditional sentences.^[Peled, _Conditional structures in Classical Arabic_ 14--15. See also footnote\ 5 on p.\ 15]

In general, all four options will have more-or-less the same meaning:
[If you come to me, I will come to you]{.trans}.
In @sec-jsh_tense below,
we will discuss the tense indicated by conditional sentences in more detail.
But for now we can generally consider
the [mADI]{.trn2} verb in a conditional sentence to lose its past tense.

For convenience,
in this,
and the following sections,
we will 
use
[قَتَلَ]{.ar}
to
refer to a [mADI]{.trn2} verb form
in either the
condition-verb
or the
condition-response-verb.
Similarly,
we will use [يَقْتُلُ]{.ar}, [يَقْتُلَ]{.ar} and [يَقْتُلْ]{.ar} to refer to
u-case, a-case, and ø-case [muDArie]{.trn2} verbs respectively.

Of the four options in examples (@ex001158) through (@ex001161),
the combinations
[إِنْ يَقْتُلْ يَقْتُلْ]{.ar}
and
[إِنْ قَتَلَ قَتَلَ]{.ar}
are most preferred.
This is because they exhibit
a symmetry between the
condition-verb
and the
condition-response-verb.^[[[كتاب سيبويه]{.ar} 3/91](https://shamela.ws/book/23018/944) cited by Peled, _Conditional structures in Classical Arabic_ 7--8]


The combination
[إِنْ قَتَلَ يَقْتُلْ]{.ar},
however,
is by no means uncommon.

But combination
[إِنْ يَقْتُلْ قَتَلَ]{.ar}
is the least commonly
found
in actual usage.
This is because when the
condition-verb
is
[يَقْتُلْ]{.ar}
it prefers the presence of
another
[يَقْتُلْ]{.ar}
after it as the condition-response-verb.^[[[كتاب سيبويه]{.ar} 3/66](https://shamela.ws/book/23018/919#p1)]
Nevertheless,
this combination
is occasionally found,
as we show in example (@ex001173) below.


With regards to the government of the conditional sentences in examples (@ex001159) through (@ex001161),
The conditional-device [إِنْ]{.ar} will continue to govern
the condition-verb and the condition-response-verb in the ø-case directly,
regardless of whether the verbs are [يَقْتُلْ]{.ar} or [قَتَلَ]{.ar}.
For a [قَتَلَ]{.ar} verb, [إِنْ]{.ar} will govern it in the positional ø-case.^[[[النحو الوافي]{.ar} 4/22](https://shamela.ws/book/10641/2354)]

In other words,
for example (@ex001159) above,
[إِنْ]{.ar} does not govern the verbal sentences
[أَتَيْتَنِي]{.ar}
and
[أَكْرَمْتُكَ]{.ar} in the positional ø-case.
Rather,
the [mADI]{.trn2} verbs
[أَتَى]{.ar} and [أَكْرَمَ]{.ar}
are,
both times,
directly governed in the positional ø-case.^[[[شرح ألفية ابن مالك للحازمي]{.ar} 113/1](https://shamela.ws/book/36130/2310)]

@fig-in_ataytani_ataytuka depicts the government of example (@ex001159).

::: {#fig-in_ataytani_ataytuka .test-class}

### Negating the condition or condition-response {#sec-jsh_negating_fil_shart}

When either of
the condition-verb or the condition-response-verb
are to be negated,
then we have two options:

 i. [لَا يَقْتُلْ]{.ar}
ii. [لَمْ يَقْتُلْ]{.ar}

<!--
The [mADI]{.trn2} verb
(with the negater [مَا]{.ar})
and the a-case [muDArie]{.trn2} verb (with [لَنْ]{.ar})
-->
Negations
[مَا قَتَلَ]{.ar}
and
[لَنْ يَقْتُلَ]{.ar}
are not used when negating
the condition-verb or the condition-response-verb.^[[[النحو الوافي]{.ar} 4/445](https://shamela.ws/book/10641/2372#p1)]
(They can however be used when negating a verb
which is not directly
the condition-verb or the condition-response-verb, as we will see in @sec-jsh_examples_of_iqtiran_fa, if Allāh wills.)

[لَا يَقْتُلْ]{.ar}
is considered the negative counterpart of
[يَقْتُلْ]{.ar}.
And
[لَمْ يَقْتُلْ]{.ar}
is considered the negative counterpart of
[قَتَلَ]{.ar}.
And as with positive conditional sentences,
a symmetry between
the condition-verb and the condition-response
is preferred.

So if the condition is
[إِنْ قَتَلَ]{.ar},
then
[لَمْ يَقْتُلْ]{.ar}
is preferred in the condition-response.^[[[شرح كتاب سيبويه للسيرافي]{.ar} 3/295](https://shamela.ws/book/17726/1291)]
For example:

(@ex001174) [إِنْ أَتَيْتَنِي لَمْ آتِكَ]{.ar}
    [composed from [[شرح كتاب سيبويه للسيرافي]{.ar} 3/295](https://shamela.ws/book/17726/1291)]{.citex}  
    [If you come to me, I will not come to you.]{.trans}

And
if the condition is
[إِنْ يَقْتُلْ]{.ar},
then
[لَا يَقْتُلْ]{.ar}
is preferred in the condition-response.^[[[شرح كتاب سيبويه للسيرافي]{.ar} 3/295](https://shamela.ws/book/17726/1291)]
For example:

(@ex001175) [إِنْ تَأْتِنِي لَا آتِكَ]{.ar}
    [composed from [[شرح كتاب سيبويه للسيرافي]{.ar} 3/295](https://shamela.ws/book/17726/1291)]{.citex}  
    [If you come to me, I will not come to you.]{.trans}


The non-symmetric combination
[إِنْ لَمْ يَقْتُلْ  يَقْتُلْ]{.ar},
(corresponding to
[إِنْ قَتَلَ  يَقْتُلْ]{.ar}),
is also fairly common.
For example:

(@ex001176) [إِنْ لَمْ تَأْتِنِي أَجْزِكَ]{.ar}
    [[[كتاب سيبويه]{.ar} 3/68](https://shamela.ws/book/23018/921)]{.citex}  
    [If you don't come to me, I will recompense you.]{.trans}

But as with the combination
[إِنْ يَقْتُلْ  قَتَلَ]{.ar}
in @sec-jsh_qatala above,
the combination
[إِنْ يَقْتُلْ  لَمْ يَقْتُلْ]{.ar}
is uncommon.
For example:

(@ex001177) [إِنْ تَأْتِنِي لَمْ آتِكَ]{.ar}
    [[[شرح كتاب سيبويه للسيرافي]{.ar} 3/295](https://shamela.ws/book/17726/1291)]{.citex}  
    [If you come to me, I will not come to you.]{.trans}

In any case,
symmetry is by no means mandatory,
and the longer the distance (in words) between
the condition-verb and the condition-response,
the easier it is to disregard its being preferred.^[[[شرح كتاب سيبويه للرماني - جزء منه]{.ar} 951](https://shamela.ws/book/18282/786#np787_3)]

With regards to
their frequencies in attested usage,
option (i)
[لَا يَقْتُلْ]{.ar}
is possibly the more original,^[Peled, _Conditional structures in Classical Arabic_ 17]
but it is rarer in usage.
Here are some examples:

(@ex001178) [إِلَّا تَفۡعَلُوهُ تَكُن فِتۡنَةࣱ فِی ٱلۡأَرۡضِ وَفَسَادࣱ كَبِیرࣱ]{.quran}
    [[[سورة الأنفال]{.ar} 8:73](https://quran.com/8/73) cited by Reckendorf, _Arabische syntax_ 487]{.citex}  
    [If you do not do so [i.e., ally yourselves with other believers], there will be fitnah [i.e., disbelief and oppression] on earth and great corruption.]{.trans}  

(@ex001179) [إِنْ تَدْفِنُوا الدَّاءَ **لَا نُخْفِهِ**]{.ar}
    [Reckendorf, _Arabische syntax_ 487]{.citex}  
    [If you bury the rancor, we will not conceal it]{.trans}  

(@ex001180) [**إِنْ لَا تَكُنْ** هِنْدٌ بَكَتْهُ فَقَدْ بَكَتْ عَلَيْهِ الثُّرَيَّا]{.ar}
    [Reckendorf, _Arabische syntax_ 487]{.citex}  
    [If Hind did not weep [for] him, then the Pleiades have wept over him]{.trans}  
    (The condition-response in this example begins with [فَ]{.ar}. We will discuss this in @sec-j_sh_msc below.)  

(@ex001181) [اللهُمّ إنْ تَظْهَرْ عَلَيّ هَذِهِ الْعِصَابَةُ يَظْهَرْ الشّرْكُ، **وَلَا يَقُمْ** لَك دِين]{.ar}
    [[[مغازي الواقدي]{.ar} 1/67](https://shamela.ws/book/23680/108) cited by Peled, _Conditional structures in Classical Arabic_ 15]{.citex}  
    [O Allāh if this band should gain ascendancy over me, polytheism would gain ascendancy, and a religion would not be established for you.]{.trans}  

(@ex001182) [وَإِنْ لَا تَفْعَلْ مَلَأْتُ يَدَكَ شُغْلًا وَلَمْ أَسُدَّ فَقْرَكَ]{.ar}
    [[[صحيح ابن حبان]{.ar} :393](https://hadithunlocked.com/ibnhibban:393)]{.citex}  
    [And if you don't do [so], I will fill your hand with preoccupation, and I will not block your poverty.]{.trans}  


The particle [لَا]{.ar}
will not affect the government of
the condition-verb or the condition-response-verb.
The conditional particle [إِنْ]{.ar} will continue to govern these verbs directly in the ø-case.
@fig-in_laa depicts the government of the negated condition-response-verb in example (@ex001179) above.

::: {#fig-in_laa .test-class}

```{.tikz}
\usetikzlibrary{decorations.text, decorations.pathreplacing}
\begin{tikzpicture}%[nodes={text depth=0.25ex,text height=1.25ex}]
\path [decoration={text effects along path, 
  text=\txarb{نُخْفِهِ} \txarb{لَا} \txarb{الدَّاءَ} \txarb{تَدْفِنُوا} \txarb{إِنْ},
  text effects/.cd, 
    path from text, text along path,
    text depth=0.25ex,text height=1.25ex,
    group letters, word count=\w,
    every word/.style={name=word-\w, execute at begin node=\strut}},
  decorate] (0,0);

%\draw [decoration={brace, mirror}, decorate] 
%   (word-5.south west) -- (word-5.south east)
%      node [midway, below, text centered,text width=1cm, xshift=10pt, yshift=-5pt] {\scriptsize conditional particle};
\draw [decoration={brace, mirror}, decorate] 
   ([xshift=1em]word-4.south west) -- (word-4.south east)
      node [midway, below, text centered,text width=1cm, xshift=0em, yshift=-5pt] {\scriptsize condition-verb};
\draw [decoration={brace, mirror}, decorate] 
   ([xshift=0.75em]word-1.south west) -- (word-1.south east)
      node [midway, below, text centered,text width=1cm, xshift=0em, yshift=-5pt] {\scriptsize condition-response-verb};

\draw[->,decorate] ([xshift=1pt] word-5.north) to [in=90,out=90,looseness=1] node[midway,inner sep=0.5pt,fill=white] {\scriptsize ø} ([xshift=0pt,yshift=1pt] word-4.north);
\draw[->,decorate] ([xshift=2pt] word-5.north) to [in=90,out=90,looseness=1] node[midway,inner sep=0.5pt,fill=white] {\scriptsize ø} ([xshift=0pt,yshift=1pt] word-1.north);

\end{tikzpicture}

```

:::

Compared to option\ (i)
[لَا يَقْتُلْ]{.ar},
option\ (ii)
[لَمْ يَقْتُلْ]{.ar}
is by far the more common technique to negate
the condition-verb and the condition-response-verb.

Just like the case for [قَتَلَ]{.ar},
when
[لَمْ]{.ar} is used to negate
the condition-verb or the condition-response-verb,
it also generally loses its past tense.

Here are some examples of
the condition-verb and the condition-response-verb,
negated with [لَمْ]{.ar}:


(@ex001183) [إِنْ أَتَيْتَنِي لَمْ آتِكَ]{.ar}
    [[[كتاب سيبويه]{.ar} 3/91](https://shamela.ws/book/23018/944)]{.citex}  
    [If you come to me, I will not come to you.]{.trans}  

(@ex001184) [إِنْ لَمْ تَأْتِنِي أَجْزِكَ]{.ar}
    [[[كتاب سيبويه]{.ar} 3/68](https://shamela.ws/book/23018/921)]{.citex}  
    [If you don't come to me, I will recompense you.]{.trans}  

(@ex001185) [إِنْ لَمْ ُتُكْرِمْنِي لَمْ أُكْرِمْكَ]{.ar}
    [[[شرح ألفية ابن مالك للشاطبي]{.ar} 6/133](https://shamela.ws/book/20562/3520)]{.citex}  
    [If you don't honor me, I will not honor you.]{.trans}  

(@ex001186) [إِنِ افْتَرَقْتُمْ **لَمْ تَجْتَمِعُوا** أَبَدًا]{.ar}
    [[[تاريخ الطبري]{.ar} 4/24](https://shamela.ws/book/9783/1915) cited by Reckendorf, _Arabische syntax_ 485]{.citex}  
    [If you factionate, you will not be united ever.]{.trans}  

(@ex001187) [وَإِنْ لَمْ يَعْمَلْهَا كُتِبَتْ حَسَنَةً]{.ar}
    [[[مسند أحمد]{.ar} :2001](https://hadithunlocked.com/ahmad:2001)]{.citex}  
    [And if he did not do it, a good deed is written for him.]{.trans}  

(@ex001188) [فَإِنْ وَجَدْتُ بُكَاءً بَكَيْتُ **وَإِنْ لَمْ أَجِدْ** بُكَاءً تَبَاكَيْتُ لِبُكَائِكُمَا]{.ar}
    [[[صحيح مسلم]{.ar} :1763](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1763)]{.citex}  
    [For if I feel like crying I will cry, and if I don't feel like crying, I will compel myself to cry [in sympathy] to your crying.]{.trans}  

The grammarians differed regarding
the government of the 
the condition-verb and the condition-response-verb,
when negated with [لَمْ]{.ar}.^[[[النحو الوافي]{.ar} 4/414--415](https://shamela.ws/book/10641/2346)]
Some grammarians are of the opinion that
[لَمْ]{.ar} directly governs the ø-case mudarie verb
while [إِنْ]{.ar} governs the verbal sentences which contain the [muDArie]{.trn2} verb.
This government is depicted in
@fig-gov_in_lam_a for example (@ex001183).

::: {#fig-gov_in_lam_a .test-class}

```{.tikz}

  text=\txarb{آتِكَ} \txarb{لَمْ} \txarb{تَأْتِنِي} \txarb{لَمْ} \txarb{إِنْ},
  text effects/.cd, 
    path from text, text along path,
    text depth=0.25ex,text height=1.25ex,
    group letters, word count=\w,
    every word/.style={name=word-\w, execute at begin node=\strut}},
  decorate] (0,0);

\draw [decoration={brace,raise=2em}, decorate] 
   (word-1.north west) -- (word-2.north east)
      node [midway, above] {};
\draw [decoration={brace,raise=2em}, decorate]

      node [midway, above] {};

\draw [decoration={brace, mirror}, decorate] 
   ([xshift=1.1em]word-3.south west) -- (word-3.south east)
      node [midway, below, text centered,text width=1cm, xshift=0em, yshift=-5pt] {\scriptsize condition-verb};
\draw [decoration={brace, mirror}, decorate] 
   ([xshift=0.85em]word-1.south west) -- (word-1.south east)
      node [midway, below, text centered,text width=1cm, xshift=0em, yshift=-5pt] {\scriptsize condition-response-verb};

\draw[->,decorate] ([xshift=1pt] word-4.north) to [in=90,out=90,looseness=2] node[midway,inner sep=0.5pt,fill=white] {\scriptsize ø} ([xshift=.5em,yshift=0.3em] word-3.north);
\draw[->,decorate] ([xshift=1pt] word-2.north) to [in=90,out=90,looseness=2] node[midway,inner sep=0.5pt,fill=white] {\scriptsize ø} ([xshift=.5em,yshift=0.3em] word-1.north);

\draw[->,decorate] ([xshift=1pt] word-5.north) to [in=90,out=90,looseness=2] node[midway,inner sep=0.5pt,fill=white] {\scriptsize ø} ([xshift=-1.5em,yshift=2.5em] word-4.north);
\draw[->,decorate] ([xshift=2pt] word-5.north) to [in=90,out=90,looseness=2] node[midway,inner sep=0.5pt,fill=white] {\scriptsize ø} ([xshift=1em,yshift=2.5em] word-1.north);

\draw [dashed] ([xshift=-1pt]word-3.north west) -- ([xshift=-1pt,yshift=2em]word-3.north west);
\draw [dashed] (word-1.north west) -- ([yshift=2em]word-1.north west);
\draw [dashed] (word-4.north east) -- ([yshift=2em]word-4.north east);
```

Other grammarians were of the opinion that [إِنْ]{.ar} would continue to govern
the condition-verb and the condition-response-verb directly,
and that [لَمْ]{.ar} has no governing effect in this case.
This is depicted in
@fig-gov_in_lam_b for the same example (@ex001183).

::: {#fig-gov_in_lam_b .test-class}

```{.tikz}
    every word/.style={name=word-\w, execute at begin node=\strut}},

   ([xshift=1.1em]word-3.south west) -- (word-3.south east)
      node [midway, below, text centered,text width=1cm, xshift=0em, yshift=-5pt] {\scriptsize condition-verb};
\draw [decoration={brace, mirror}, decorate]

      node [midway, below, text centered,text width=1cm, xshift=0em, yshift=-5pt] {\scriptsize condition-response-verb};

\draw[->,decorate] ([xshift=1pt] word-5.north) to [in=90,out=90,looseness=1] node[midway,inner sep=0.5pt,fill=white] {\scriptsize ø} ([xshift=.25em,yshift=.5em] word-3.north);
\draw[->,decorate] ([xshift=2pt] word-5.north) to [in=90,out=90,looseness=1] node[midway,inner sep=0.5pt,fill=white] {\scriptsize ø} ([xshift=0.25em,yshift=.5em] word-1.north);

```

:::

### The inverted conditional sentence {#sec-jsh_inverted_in}

<!--
[[النحو الوافي]{.ar} 4/450-451 (footnote); Peled, _Conditional structures in Classical Arabic_ 139--140; [شرح ابن يعيش على المفصل]{.ar} 5/118]
-->

Oftentimes,
we come across an _inverted_ conditional sentence,
where what seems to be the condition-response comes before the condition.
For example:

(@ex001189) [آتِيكَ إِنْ أَتَيْتَنِى]{.ar}
    [[[شرح ابن يعيش على المفصل]{.ar} 5/118](https://shamela.ws/book/13301/2056)]{.citex}  
    [I will come to you if you come to me.]{.trans}  

In example (@ex001189) above, it would seem that
[آتِيكَ]{.ar}
is the condition-response
and
[إِنْ أَتَيْتَنِى]{.ar}
is the condition.

But actually,
the mainstream view amongst the grammarians is that
[آتِيكَ]{.ar}
cannot be a condition-response because the
condition-response is not allowed to precede the condition.

This view is supported by the fact that the
verb in
[آتِيكَ]{.ar}
is in the u-case.
If it were a condition-response-verb then it would be in the ø-case, thus:
[آتِكَ]{.ar}.
But
a ø-case [muDArie]{.trn2} verb in the beginning of sentence,
followed by a condition is not a correctly formed sentence.
So we cannot say, for example:

(@ex001190) ✗ [آتِكَ إِنْ أَتَيْتَنِى]{.ar}
    [[[شرح ابن يعيش على المفصل]{.ar} 5/118](https://shamela.ws/book/13301/2056)]{.citex}  

The way the grammarians solve
the analysis of example (@ex001189) is
by considering
[آتِيكَ]{.ar}
an independent sentence
that is
structurally complete.
[إِنْ أَتَيْتَنِى]{.ar}
is then considered to be a condition.
Its
condition-response
[[آتِكَ]]{.ar}
is [taqdIr]{.trn2}ed
after it.
The [taqdIr]{.trn2}ed condition-response
is deleted in surface speech
and its meaning is indicated by the preceding independent sentence
[آتِيكَ]{.ar}.

The complete sentence with the [taqdIr]{.trn2} is:

(@ex001191) [آتِيكَ إِنْ أَتَيْتَنِى [آتِكَ]]{.ar}

<!--
The [taqdIr]{.trn2} of the deleted condition-response is 
[آتِكَ]{.ar}.
This rendition of the [taqdIr]{.trn2} is suggested by the preceding independent sentence
[آتِيكَ]{.ar}.
-->

But how is the conditional sentence
[إِنْ أَتَيْتَنِى [آتِكَ]]{.ar}
connected
to the preceding independent sentence
[آتِيكَ]{.ar}?
One opinion
is that the conditional sentence
[إِنْ أَتَيْتَنِى [آتِكَ]]{.ar}
can be considered to be
pertinent to
the verb in
[آتِيكَ]{.ar}
in much the same way as an adverb of time/place or preposition would be,^[[[شرح ابن يعيش على المفصل]{.ar} 5/118](https://shamela.ws/book/13301/2056)]
for example, in:

(@ex001192) [آتيك يومَ الجمعة]{.ar}
    [[[شرح ابن يعيش على المفصل]{.ar} 5/118](https://shamela.ws/book/13301/2056)]{.citex}  
    [I will come to you the day of Friday.]{.trans}  

<!--
@fig-inverted_shart depicts this theorized government of example ().

TODO: think about if [إِنْ]{.ar} itself should be governed by [يَقْتُلُ]{.ar} and not the entire conditional sentence.
Then it will be more in line with prepositions.
But then how about sentences like
[اضرب مَنْ يقُمْ]{.ar},
if indeed they are valid?
On the other hand [آتيك في البيت]{.ar} is similar to [آتيك عند البيت]{.ar}, so then [في]{.ar}
(and [إِنْ]{.ar}) should be governed directly by the verb.


::: {#fig-inverted_shart .test-class}

Having said all the above,
there is no problem if we refer to sentences like example (@ex001189)
[آتِيكَ إِنْ أَتَيْتَنِى]{.ar}
loosely speaking and for convenience,
as inverted conditional sentences.
As long as we understand that the true condition-response is deleted and [taqdIr]{.trn2}ed after the condition in sentence word order.

Here are some more examples of inverted conditional sentences:


(@ex001193) [أًحْسِنُ إليك إن أكرمتَنى]{.ar}
    [[[شرح ابن يعيش على المفصل]{.ar} 5/118](https://shamela.ws/book/13301/2056)]{.citex}  
    [I will be good to you if you honor me.]{.trans}  

(@ex001194) [أنتِ طالقٌ إن دخلتِ الدارَ]{.ar}
    [[[شرح ابن يعيش على المفصل]{.ar} 5/118](https://shamela.ws/book/13301/2056)]{.citex}  
    [You~f~ are divorced if you enter the house.]{.trans}  

(@ex001195) [أنا ظالمٌ إن فعلتُ]{.ar}
    [[[شرح ابن يعيش على المفصل]{.ar} 5/118](https://shamela.ws/book/13301/2056)]{.citex}  
    [I [will be] a wrongdoer if I did [some action].]{.trans}  

(@ex001196) [لاَ يَقُلْ أَحَدُكُمُ **اللَّهُمَّ اغْفِرْ لِي إِنْ شِئْتَ ارْحَمْنِي إِنْ شِئْتَ ارْزُقْنِي إِنْ شِئْتَ** وَلْيَعْزِمْ مَسْأَلَتَهُ إِنَّهُ يَفْعَلُ مَا يَشَاءُ لاَ مُكْرِهَ لَهُ]{.ar}
    [[[صحيح البخاري]{.ar} :7477](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:7477)]{.citex}  
    [Let not any of you say, **"O Allāh, forgive me if You wish, have mercy on me if You wish, provide sustenance me if You wish."** [Rather,] let him be resolved in his asking. Indeed He does what He wills, there is no one to compel Him.]{.trans}

In examples (@ex001194) and (@ex001195) above,
the "inverted" condition-responses
are the nounal sentences
([أَنْتِ طَالِقٌ]{.ar}
and
[أَنَا ظَالِمٌ]{.ar}), not verbal sentences.
We will discuss such condition-responses in @sec-jsh_examples_of_iqtiran_fa, if Allāh wills.


Note that all the examples
of inverted conditional sentences,
that we have given so far
have
[إِنْ قَتَلَ]{.ar}
in the condition
and not
[إِنْ يَقْتُلْ]{.ar}.
This is because,
as we mentioned in @sec-jsh_qatala above,
when the
condition-verb
is
[يَقْتُلْ]{.ar}
it prefers the presence of
another
[يَقْتُلْ]{.ar}
after it as the condition-response-verb.
So the following example is not preferred:

(@ex001197) [آتِيكَ إِنْ تَأْتِنِي]{.ar}
    [[[كتاب سيبويه]{.ar} 3/68](https://shamela.ws/book/23018/921); [[شرح ابن يعيش على المفصل]{.ar} 5/118](https://shamela.ws/book/13301/2056)]{.citex}  
    [I will come to you, if you come to me.]{.trans}  

This is because
[يَقْتُلْ]{.ar}
in the condition
([إِنْ تَأْتِنِي]{.ar})
prefers 
that it have another [يَقْتُلْ]{.ar}
in the condition-response,
and that its condition-response
not be deleted.^[[[كتاب سيبويه]{.ar} 3/68](https://shamela.ws/book/23018/921); [[شرح ابن يعيش على المفصل]{.ar} 5/118](https://shamela.ws/book/13301/2056)]

Having said that, an inverted
[إِنْ يَقْتُلْ]{.ar}
condition
could very rarely be found.^[Peled, _Conditional structures in Classical Arabic_ 143]

[إِنْ لَمْ يَقْتُلْ]{.ar}
in an inverted conditional sentence
is,
however,
fine.
This is
because it is the negative counterpart to
[إِنْ قَتَلَ]{.ar}.
For example,

(@ex001198) [وَاعْلَمِي أَنِّي امْرُؤٌ سَأَمُوتُ إنْ لَمْ أُقْتَلِ]{.ar}
    [[عنترة]{.ar} cited by Reckendorf, _Arabische syntax_ 488]{.citex}  
    [Know that I am a person-- I will die if I am not killed.]{.trans}

### A u-case [muDArie]{.trn2} condition-response-verb {#sec-j_sh_jawab_ucase_wo_fa}


Occassionally we see a conditional sentence
of the form
[إِنْ قَتَلَ يَقْتُلُ]{.ar}.
That is, a [muDArie]{.trn2} condition-response-verb is in the u-case,
not the ø-case.
For example:

(@ex001199) [إِنْ أَتَيْتَنِي آتِيكَ]{.ar}
    [[[كتاب سيبويه]{.ar} 3/66](https://shamela.ws/book/23018/919#p1)]{.citex}  
    [If you come to me, I come to you.]{.trans}  

This structure again requires [taqdIr]{.trn2} to analyze it.
This is
because the underlying principle that the grammarians have theorized
for the conditional sentence,
is that
the conditional-device [إِنْ]{.ar}
governs
both the condition-verb
and the condition-response-verb
in the ø-case.

One way the grammarians work around this problem is by [taqdIr]{.trn2}ing example (@ex001199)
to essentially be an inverted conditional sentence, thus:

(@ex001200) [آتِيكَ إِنْ أَتَيْتَنِي [آتِكَ]]{.ar}  
    [I come to you if you come to me [I come to you].]{.trans}  

Once the original condition-response
[آتِكَ]{.ar}
is deleted,
then the independent sentence
[آتِيكَ]{.ar}
is (optionally)
moved to after the condition to take the place of
the original condition-response
[آتِكَ]{.ar}.^[[[النحو الوافي]{.ar} 4/475--476 (footnotes)](https://shamela.ws/book/10641/2402) citing [كتاب سيبويه]{.ar}]

There is also another technique to analyze such conditional sentences,
and that is to assume a deleted [فَ]{.ar}
(and also possibly a deleted subject)
before the condition-response.^[[[شرح كتاب سيبويه للرماني - جزء منه]{.ar} 949](https://shamela.ws/book/18282/784#p1)]
With the
deleted elements restored,
restored, the sentence is:

(@ex001201) [إِنْ أَتَيْتَنِي فَآتِيكَ]{.ar}  
    or  
    [إِنْ أَتَيْتَنِي فَأَنا آتِيكَ]{.ar}
    [composed from [[شرح كتاب سيبويه للرماني - جزء منه]{.ar} 949](https://shamela.ws/book/18282/784#p1)]{.citex}  
    [If you come to me **then** I will come to you.]{.trans}  

Condition-responses that begin with [فَ]{.ar} will be treated in @sec-j_sh_msc below, if Allāh wills.

Here are some more examples of this kind of conditional sentence:

(@ex001202) [**وإن أتاه** خليلٌ يومَ مسألةٍ **يقولُ** لا غائبٌ مالي ولا حَرِمُ]{.ar}
    [[[كتاب سيبويه]{.ar} 3/66](https://shamela.ws/book/23018/919#p1)]{.citex}  
    [And if a friend came to him on a day of asking, he says, "My wealth is neither absent nor denied."]{.trans}


Note again,
that the condition-verb in these examples has been [قَتَلَ]{.ar},
not [يَقْتُلْ]{.ar}.
This is again consistent
with what we mentioned in @sec-jsh_qatala,
that when the condition-verb is [يَقْتُلْ]{.ar}
then it prefers the presence of another [يَقْتُلْ]{.ar} as the condition-response-verb.

Having said that,
a conditional sentence of the form
[إِنْ يَقْتُلْ يَقْتُلُ]{.ar}
is found on occasion, often by poetic license.^[[[كتاب سيبويه]{.ar} 3/67](https://shamela.ws/book/23018/920#p1)]
For example:

(@ex001203) [يا أَقْرَعُ بنَ حابسٍ يا أَقْرَعُ ~ إنَّك **إن يُصْرَعْ أخوك تُصْرَعُ**]{.ar}
    [[[كتاب سيبويه]{.ar} 3/67](https://shamela.ws/book/23018/920#p1)]{.citex}  
    [O [#aqrae]{.trn2} son of [#HAbis]{.trn2}, O [#aqrae]{.trn2}! Indeed if your brother would be thrown down, you are being thrown down.]{.trans}  
    An alternate analysis is that the condition is parenthetical and [تُصْرَعُ]{.ar} is the info of [إِنَّكَ]{.ar}.^[see [[الجملة الشرطية عند النحاة العرب للشمسان]{.ar} 246](https://archive.org/details/aljomla-ashrtia.g/page/n247/mode/2up)]


(@ex001204) [قَالَتِ اللَّهُمَّ **إِنْ يَمُتْ يُقَالُ** هِيَ قَتَلَتْهُ]{.ar}
    [[[صحيح البخاري]{.ar} :2217](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:2217) cited by Peled, _Conditional structures in Classical Arabic_ 17]{.citex}  
    [She said, "O Allāh if he should die, it will be said, 'She killed him.'"]{.trans}  

<!--
### A u-case [muDArie]{.trn2} condition-verb

Exceedingly rarely,
we see a [إِنْ]{.ar} conditional sentence
with a [يَقْتُلُ]{.ar} form in the condition-verb.
That is, a [muDArie]{.trn2} condition-verb is in the u-case,
not the ø-case.
For example:

(@ex001205) [فإما ترين]{.ar}
    [[[شواهد التوضيح لابن مالك]{.ar} 72](https://shamela.ws/book/98123/69#p1)]{.citex}  
-->

### [إِمَّا]{.ar}

[مَا]{.ar} may optionaly be suffixed to [إِنْ]{.ar}.
The [ن]{.ar} is assimilated with the [م]{.ar},
and
it is then  written and pronounced as [إِمَّا]{.ar}.
By the way,
this [إِمَّا]{.ar} is distinct from the [إِمَّا]{.ar} that is used to signify
[either\ ... or]{.trans}.^[[[مغني اللبيب لابن هشام]{.ar} 1/61](https://ketabonline.com/ar/books/57084/read?part=1&page=59&index=3271127)]
The addition of [مَا]{.ar} to [إِنْ]{.ar}
can emphasize the meaning of the condition-response.
Example:

(@ex001206) [إمّا تَأْتِنِي آتِكَ]{.ar}
    [[[شرح ابن يعيش على المفصل]{.ar} 5/115](https://shamela.ws/book/13301/2053)]{.citex}  
    [If you come to me, I will come to you.]{.trans}  

[يَقْتُلْ]{.ar},
as a condition-verb,
is only used with [إِمَّا]{.ar} uncommonly or by poetic license.^[[[النحو الوافي]{.ar} 4/174](https://shamela.ws/book/10641/2106)]
Instead, the condition-verb with [إِمَّا]{.ar} is usually a emphatic verb
([يَقْتُلَنَّ]{.ar}).
For example:

(@ex001207) [فَإِمَّا تَرَیِنَّ مِنَ ٱلۡبَشَرِ أَحَدࣰا فَقُولِیۤ إِنِّی نَذَرۡتُ لِلرَّحۡمَـٰنِ صَوۡمࣰا فَلَنۡ أُكَلِّمَ ٱلۡیَوۡمَ إِنسِیࣰّا]{.quran}
    [[[سورة مريم]{.ar} 19:26](https://quran.com/19/26) cited by [[شرح ابن يعيش على المفصل]{.ar} 5/115](https://shamela.ws/book/13301/2053)]{.citex}  
    [And if you see from among humanity anyone, say, 'Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful abstention, so I will not speak today to [any] man.'"]{.trans}  
    ([فَ]{.ar} introducing the condition-response is discussed in @sec-j_sh_msc below.)

## The [إِذَا]{.ar} conditional sentence {#sec-jsh_idha}

### The original temporal signification of [إِذَا]{.ar}

[إِذَا]{.ar} [when]{.trans}
is a noun which originally has a
temporal (time) signification
rather than a conditional signification.^[Peled, _Conditional structures in Classical Arabic_ 24 citing [[كتاب سيبويه]{.ar} 3/60](https://shamela.ws/book/23018/913#p1); [[المقتضب للمبرد]{.ar} 2/55-56](https://shamela.ws/book/6965/324#p1)]
For example,

(@ex001208) [آتِيكَ إِذَا احْمَرَّ الْبُسْرُ]{.ar}
    [[[كتاب سيبويه]{.ar} 3/60](https://shamela.ws/book/23018/913#p1)]{.citex}  
    [I will come to you when the unripe dates redden.]{.trans}

In example (@ex001208) above,
the
u-case [muDArie]{.trn2} verb
[آتِي]{.ar}
signifies its usual imperfect aspect
[I come/will come]{.trans}.
This is because example (@ex001208) is technically not a conditional sentence.
[إِذَا]{.ar} signifies
[when]{.trans}, not as a condition which may or may not occur,
but as an event which is expected to occur.


[إِذَا]{.ar} is in the a-case as a adverb of place.
It is governed by the verb [آتِي]{.ar}.
[إِذَا]{.ar} is also a annexed noun.
Its (positional) annexed-to noun is
the following verbal sentence
[احْمَرَّ الْبُسْرُ]{.ar}.
<!--
A word-for-word translation that indicates this government is:
[I will come to you **at the time of when** the unripe dates redden]{.trans}
-->
The government of example (@ex001208) above is depicted in @fig-aatika_idha_hmarra_lbusr.

::: {#fig-aatika_idha_hmarra_lbusr .test-class}

```{.tikz}
\usetikzlibrary{decorations.text, decorations.pathreplacing}
\begin{tikzpicture}%[nodes={text depth=0.25ex,text height=1.25ex}]
\path [decoration={text effects along path, 
  text=\txarb{الْبُسْرُ} \txarb{احْمَرَّ} \txarb{إِذَا} \txarb{آتِيكَ},
  text effects/.cd, 
    path from text, text along path,
    text depth=0.25ex,text height=1.25ex,
    group letters, word count=\w,
    every word/.style={name=word-\w, execute at begin node=\strut}},
  decorate] (0,0);

%\draw [decoration={brace, mirror}, decorate] 
%   (word-5.south west) -- (word-5.south east)
%      node [midway, below, text centered,text width=1cm, xshift=10pt, yshift=-5pt] {\scriptsize conditional particle};
%\draw [decoration={brace, mirror}, decorate] 
%   (word-3.south west) -- (word-5.south east)
%      node [midway, below, text centered,text width=1cm, yshift=-5pt] {\scriptsize condition};
\draw [decoration={brace}, decorate] 
   (word-1.north west) -- (word-2.north east)
      node [midway, above] {};

\draw[->,decorate] ([xshift=3pt] word-4.north) to [in=90,out=90,looseness=1] node[midway,inner sep=0.5pt,fill=white] {\scriptsize a} ([xshift=2pt] word-3.north);
\draw[->,decorate] ([xshift=-2pt] word-3.north) to [in=90,out=90,looseness=1] node[midway,inner sep=0.5pt,fill=white] {\scriptsize i} ([xshift=-13pt,yshift=4pt] word-2.north);

%\path (0,0) node [midway, below=7.5ex, right=0ex, align=left] {``I read the small books.''};

\end{tikzpicture}
```

:::

A [قَتَلَ]{.ar} verbal sentence
typically does not hold on to its past tense
when it is the positional annexed-to noun of
[إِذَا]{.ar}.
That is why we have translated
[احْمَرَّ]{.ar} in example (@ex001208) as
[redden]{.trans},
not [reddened]{.trans}.

<!--
[إِذَا]{.ar} usually indicates a future time.
[إِذَا]{.ar} is also most commonly followed by a [mADI]{.trn2} verb
in its positional annexed-to noun,
(like [احْمَرَّ]{.ar} in example () above).
But because of the future signification of [إِذَا]{.ar} the [mADI]{.trn2} verb will (usually) give a future meaning:
[when the unripe dates [**will**] redden]{.trans}.

The past tense equivalent of example () above is:

(@ex001209) [أَتَيْتُكَ إِذِ احْمَرَّ الْبُسْرُ]{.ar}  
    [I **came** to you when the unripe dates **reddened**.]{.trans}

The adverb of place
[إِذْ]{.ar}
usually indicates a past time just like
[إِذَا]{.ar} usually indicates a future time.
-->

### Conditional signification of [إِذَا]{.ar}

Example (@ex001208) above can be transformed into a conditional sentence.
This is done by taking [إِذَا]{.ar} and its positional annexed-to noun
[احْمَرَّ الْبُسْرُ]{.ar},
and putting them in the front of
the sentence,
<!--
the verbal sentence
[آتِيكَ]{.ar},
-->
thus:

(@ex001210) [إِذَا احْمَرَّ الْبُسْرُ أَتَيْتُكَ]{.ar}  
    [When the unripe dates redden, I will come to you.]{.trans}

Note that we have also replaced the [يَقْتُلُ]{.ar} verbal sentence
[آتِيكَ]{.ar} in example (@ex001208)
with the [قَتَلَ]{.ar} verbal sentence
[أَتَيْتُ]{.ar}.
This is because
now that example (@ex001210) is a conditional sentence
(with the condition-response following
the condition),
[قَتَلَ]{.ar} as the condition-response-verb also does not hold on to its past tense meaning.

<!--
This is because when [إِذَا]{.ar} is a conditional-device in a conditional sentence,
then, like [إِنْ]{.ar},
it requires verbal sentences in both the condition and the condition-response.
But whereas [إِنْ]{.ar} allows both (ø-case) [muDArie]{.trn2} verbs and [mADI]{.trn2} verbs,
[إِذَا]{.ar} strongly prefers [mADI]{.trn2} verbs in both clauses.
Because of the typical future signification of [إِذَا]{.ar},
both [mADI]{.trn2} verbs will usually have a future meaning.
-->

Also unlike [إِنْ]{.ar}, 
even when [إِذَا]{.ar} is a conditional-device,
it does not (directly) govern either of the verbs in the condition or the condition-response.
Rather, [إِذَا]{.ar} governs entire verbal sentence in the condition in an annexation.
And [إِذَا]{.ar} itself is governed by the verb in the condition-response.^[Some grammarians disagreed. Give Abu Hayyan's opinion.]
@fig-idha_hmarra_lbusru_ataytuka
depicts the government of example (@ex001210).

::: {#fig-idha_hmarra_lbusru_ataytuka .test-class}

```{.tikz}

  text=\txarb{أَتَيْتُكَ} \txarb{الْبُسْرُ} \txarb{احْمَرَّ} \txarb{إِذَا},
  text effects/.cd, 
    path from text, text along path,
    text depth=0.25ex,text height=1.25ex,
    group letters, word count=\w,
    every word/.style={name=word-\w, execute at begin node=\strut}},
  decorate] (0,0);

%\draw [decoration={brace, mirror}, decorate] 
%   (word-5.south west) -- (word-5.south east)
%      node [midway, below, text centered,text width=1cm, xshift=10pt, yshift=-5pt] {\scriptsize conditional particle};
\draw [decoration={brace, mirror}, decorate] 
   (word-2.south west) -- (word-4.south east)
      node [midway, below, text centered,text width=1cm, xshift=5pt, yshift=-5pt] {\scriptsize condition};
\draw [decoration={brace, mirror}, decorate] 
   (word-1.south west) -- (word-1.south east)
      node [midway, below, text centered,text width=1cm, xshift=-5pt, yshift=-5pt] {\scriptsize condition-response};
\draw [decoration={brace}, decorate] 
   (word-2.north west) -- (word-3.north east)
      node [midway, above] {};

\draw[->,decorate] ([xshift=3pt] word-1.north) to [in=90,out=90,looseness=1] node[midway,inner sep=0.5pt,fill=white] {\scriptsize a} ([xshift=2pt] word-4.north);
\draw[->,decorate] ([xshift=-2pt] word-4.north) to [in=90,out=90,looseness=1] node[midway,inner sep=0.5pt,fill=white] {\scriptsize i} ([xshift=-13pt,yshift=4pt] word-3.north);

%\path (0,0) node [midway, below=7.5ex, right=0ex, align=left] {``I read the small books.''};
```
